title: A role for CIZ1, a Nuclear Matrix Protein Overexpressed in Cancer Cells, in Controlling the Initiation of DNA Replication.
authors: Hossain, Manzar; Tramantano, Michael; Naik, Sanjay; Stillman, Bruce
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: DNA replication licensing is tightly coordinated with cell-cycle progression to ensure genome stability. Here we demonstrate that CIZ1, a nuclear matrix scaffold protein in human cells, coordinates DNA replication licensing through direct interactions with the Origin Recognition Complex (ORC), CDC6, and Cyclins E/A-CDK2. The C-terminal zinc finger region of CIZ1 mediates binding to the cyclin-binding motifs of ORC1 and CDC6, and Cyclin-CDK-dependent phosphorylation regulates these interactions. Cell cycle analyses demonstrated a dynamic association of CIZ1 with ORC1 and CDC6. Functional studies showed that CIZ1 depletion impaired MCM loading, reduced DNA synthesis, delayed S-phase progression and inhibited cell proliferation. Cancer cells overexpressing CIZ1 exhibited an enhanced dependency on its expression, and CRISPR tiling screens identified the C-terminal regulatory region containing cyclin-binding motifs and CDK phosphorylation sites as essential for cell proliferation. Acute degradation of CIZ1 further revealed an unexpected role in maintaining CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) occupancy at specific genomic loci and regulating transcriptional programs associated with cell adhesion and migration, indicating that CIZ1 links DNA replication with higher-order genome organization. Finally, depletion of CIZ1 significantly suppressed colorectal tumor growth in xenograft models. Together, these findings establish CIZ1 as a multifunctional scaffold that integrates DNA replication licensing, Cyclin- CDK signaling, and chromatin architecture.

title: Guanine content in the CTCF motif encodes a vulnerability to persistent, alcohol-induced redistribution.
authors: Nolan, Ben; Puspo, Joynob A; Querry-Peterson, Iesha M; Maurina, Stephanie; Wright, Rebecca A; Schmitz, Allyson; Jacobsen, Lauren E; Ortiz, Coralmarie; Reznicek, Timothy E; Ethell, Alexander; Harris, Hannah L; Cummings, Christopher T; Rowley, M Jordan
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Alcohol consumption is a leading contributor to the global disease burden, yet its molecular consequences remain incompletely understood. Ethanol's first metabolite, acetaldehyde, modifies guanine to form DNA adducts and DNA-protein crosslinks that block elongating RNA polymerase II. Because acetaldehyde acts specifically on guanine, we hypothesized that chromatin features would be disrupted in a sequence-dependent rather than stochastic manner. Here we confirm that alcohol exposure displaces elongating RNA polymerase II (RNAPIIs2p) from gene bodies, relocating to promoters. In addition to this confirmation, we found that RNAPIIs2p also relocates to discrete guanine-rich intergenic CTCF sites. Loci with high guanine content at the CTCF motif's zinc finger 5 (ZF5) binding position showed the largest increase in both CTCF and cohesin (RAD21), with CTCF occupancy changes persisting even six days after alcohol withdrawal. Surprisingly, using Hi-C, we found that these changes to CTCF and cohesin do not impact the pronounced structural CTCF loops, but are instead primarily associated with altered guanine-rich enhancer-promoter contacts that connect to lasting changes to gene expression. Beyond our cell-line model, the same sequence rule accounts for altered CTCF occupancy in a mouse starvation (metabolic stress) model and in the placentae after paternal alcohol exposure. Together these findings link alcohol exposure to sequence-directed changes to chromatin whose rules are conserved in alcohol-associated disease.

title: Transcriptomic Identification of Candidate Biomarkers Associated With Vascular Calcification-Related Signaling Pathways in Immunoglobulin A Nephropathy.
authors: Cheng, LiJuan; Xin, ZiJin; Zhao, XinLi; Wang, JingFeng
abstract: BACKGROUND: Immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) is one of the most prevalent primary glomerular diseases globally. This study is aimed at identifying candidate biomarkers associated with vascular calcification-related signaling pathways in IgAN and at investigating their potential biological associations. METHODS: This was an observational bioinformatics study based on public transcriptomic datasets. Vascular calcification-related genes (VCRGs) were defined based on selected KEGG signaling pathways. Data were obtained from public databases. Candidate biomarkers were identified via differential analysis, machine learning, and cross-compartment external expression assessment. Enrichment analysis, immune infiltration, regulatory networks, computational drug prediction, and computational N6-methyladenosine (m6A) site prediction were used to explore the potential biological context of the candidate biomarkers. RESULTS: Differential analysis identified 348 differentially expressed genes (DEGs). By intersecting these DEGs with VCRGs, 30 candidate genes were obtained. JUN, FOS, and COL1A2 were finally identified as candidate biomarkers, and these genes were mainly associated with the "Nagashima EGF signaling" and "Nagashima NRG1 signaling." Six differential immune cell types (e.g., M2 macrophages) differed significantly between the IgAN and control groups. Spearman analysis showed that COL1A2 was negatively correlated with resting natural killer (NK) cells (cor = -0.57, p < 0.05); and FOS was positively correlated with resting NK cells (cor = 0.72, p < 0.01). BRD4, MAZ, and CTCF were computationally predicted as shared candidate transcription factors (TFs). A regulatory association involving hsa-miR-139-5p and FOS was also predicted. Troglitazone was predicted to target JUN. High-confidence m6A modification sites were computationally predicted in all three candidate biomarkers. These findings were considered exploratory and hypothesis generating. CONCLUSION: JUN, FOS, and COL1A2 were identified as IgAN-associated candidate biomarkers linked to vascular calcification-related signaling pathway genes, providing exploratory biological insights into the potential molecular links between IgAN and calcification-related signaling.

title: Specification of Origins of DNA Replication Within Distinct Chromatin States in Human Cells.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: A comprehensive map of binding sites for the Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) in the human genome reveals relationships among replication licensing, chromatin state, three-dimensional genome organization, location of origins of DNA replication and DNA replication timing. Defining these relationships is essential for understanding how replication licensing is integrated with the broader organization and duplication of the human genome. Using 30 high-quality ORC1 CUT&RUN datasets, an ORC1 three-dimensional binding matrix (ORC1 3DM) was constructed that captures genomic position, binding intensity, and reproducibility across replicates. This analysis reveals considerable heterogeneity in ORC1 binding, and integration with chromatin-state maps shows that ORC1-binding sites separate into distinct epigenomic groups, with high-confidence sites enriched in H2A.Z1- and H3K4me3-associated open chromatin. Hi-C analysis demonstrates preferential localization of ORC1 binding to sub-regions of genomic A compartments and frequent association with loop anchors, supported by a direct interaction between ORC1 and CTCF. Replication-timing analysis shows that ORC1-binding sites are enriched in initiation zones and exhibit subgroup-specific temporal patterns. An integrated analysis combining multiple replication initiation assays and chromatin features further places ORC1 3DM within a unified replication-chromatin framework. Together, these results support a hierarchical, probabilistic model of replication licensing that is embedded within chromatin architecture. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: Understanding how DNA replication licensing relates to chromatin organization requires quantitative mapping and integration of genomic features. We developed an ORC1 three-dimensional binding matrix (ORC1 3DM) from 30 CUT&RUN datasets, quantifying genomic binding coordinates, intensity and reproducibility. We established an integrative framework to compare diverse genomic datasets across 25 chromatin states and a high-resolution approach to characterize replication timing profiles and their relationships with replication initiation. These approaches revealed distinct chromatin-associated ORC1-binding groups, preferential localization of high-confidence ORC1 sites in active chromatin and highly interactive A-compartment subregions, and subgroup-specific relationships with replication initiation and timing. Together, these findings and methodological advances provide a quantitative framework for investigating relationships among replication licensing, chromatin state, three-dimensional genome organization, and replication timing.

title: Evolution of CTCF underlies the establishment of loop extrusion as a predominant chromatin folding mechanism in vertebrates.
authors: Astica, Liene; Acemel, Rafael D; Schwarzenbacher, Henrike; Racioppi, Claudia; Rojas, Ana M; Rotllant, Josep; Bogdanovic, Ozren; Real, Francisca M; Christiaen, Lionel; Zinzen, Robert; Lupianez, Dario G
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: CTCF is a DNA-binding protein that emerged in the last bilaterian ancestor and that plays a central role in 3D genome organization. Yet, despite its relevance, genomic studies have revealed notable differences in CTCF function across animal clades. In vertebrates, CTCF is essential for TAD organization through cohesin-mediated loop extrusion, whereas its contribution to chromatin organization outside this clade appears to be more limited. Here we investigate the evolution of CTCF as an architectural factor through a cross-species functional replacement approach, in which orthologs from divergent bilaterian lineages are expressed in either mouse embryonic stem cells or Drosophila embryos. Chromosome conformation analyses demonstrated that the ability of CTCF to mediate loop extrusion-dependent TAD formation is encoded within the vertebrate protein. Yet, this property alone is insufficient to establish vertebrate-like genome architecture in an invertebrate background, suggesting the existence of additional lineage-specific factors. ChIP-seq analyses further revealed that CTCF DNA-binding specificity has been progressively refined during bilaterian evolution, with the vertebrate lineage exhibiting a preferential shift towards distal genomic regions that is consistent with an expansion of regulatory domains. Notably, despite failing to form TADs, the ortholog from a non-vertebrate chordate partially rescued the lethality associated with the loss of the vertebrate CTCF protein, indicating that its architectural and regulatory functions are evolutionary independent. Further Hi-C analyses in tunicate and cyclostome species suggest that the ability of CTCF to act as a loop extrusion barrier was already present in the last common ancestor of all vertebrates. Altogether, our findings establish the diversification of CTCF regulation and function as key drivers for the specialization of bilaterian 3D genome organization.

title: Engineered Tn5 Variants Enhance CUT&Tag Fidelity for Transcription Factors.
authors: Piper, Lola; Baird, Emma; Ashbaugh, Harry J; Pentecost, Olivia A; Nowinski, Sara M; Janssens, Derek H
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: The CUT&Tag method performs exceptionally well for profiling histone modifications, but mapping sequence-specific transcription factors (TFs) is complicated by intrinsic Tn5 activity at accessible DNA, and the high-salt washes used to suppress this activity can destabilize TF-chromatin interactions. We engineered the Tn5 DNA-binding channel to attenuate target-DNA engagement by replacing individual positively charged amino acids with neutral amino acids. We identified a "Goldilocks" variant (K160A) with intermediate attenuation that improved recovery of GATA2 motif-containing sites under low-salt CUT&Tag and KCl-based DynaTag conditions. A second variant (K249A) had improved performance for profiling CTCF over less accessible sites characterized by sharply focused short-fragment enrichment. By comparing the K160A and K249A variants, this TF-CUT&Tag assay provides a physical readout of the local chromatin environment at TF binding sites. Applying K160A TF-CUT&Tag to pluripotency-associated TFs in mouse embryonic stem cells increased recovery across their genomic binding landscapes while preserving factor-specific motif architectures. During skeletal muscle differentiation, TF-CUT&Tag improved recovery of MyoG and Pax7 occupancy relative to standard CUT&Tag, revealing strongly motif-enriched MyoG binding and a shift in Pax7 binding from CpG-rich promoters in progenitors toward Pax7 motif-enriched sites during differentiation. Together, these results show that TF-CUT&Tag captures distinct modes of TF- chromatin interaction, including motif-directed binding sites and more salt-sensitive sites that may depend on lower-affinity DNA recognition or protein-protein interactions and are difficult to predict from DNA sequence alone.

title: ChAI-Net learns a regulatory code for chromatin co-accessibility.
authors: Lee, Jodi; Zhang, Kaite; Shurberg, Ethan; Ramani, Vijay; Pollard, Katherine S
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: The regulation of chromatin accessibility is critical for cell function and identity. Advances in single-molecule long-read footprinting have enabled near-nucleotide-resolution readout of chromatin fiber organization, capturing both coordination of transcription factor (TF) binding and variation in nucleosome positioning previously obscured by bulk methods. Here we combine this technique with deep learning to study how protein-DNA interactions are coordinated within different types of cis -regulatory elements in mouse embryonic stem cells. First, we quantify the frequency with which pairs of positions are simultaneously accessible on individual molecules. Then, we train ChAI-Net, a neural network that predicts these locus-specific chromatin co-accessibility maps from the underlying DNA sequence. Through model interpretation and in silico experiments, we show that ChAI-Net learns unique combinations of sequence motifs underlying co-accessibility within enhancers, promoters, and CTCF-bound sites. Many of these motifs are missed when modeling average accessibility, suggesting a specific role in coordinated binding. ChAI-Net's regulatory grammar also highlights the importance of TF motif orientation, spacing, positioning, and co-occurrence in driving co-accessibility. Thus, our framework for extracting regulatory rules from footprinting data expands understanding of TF cooperativity, while laying the groundwork to elucidate how these rules vary across cellular contexts as single-molecule genomics is deployed at scale.

title: Histone modifications define distinct nucleosome positions in cell-free DNA.
authors: Ou, Yukun; Gulati, Gunsagar S; Tyndall, Caroline F; Pandey, Medha; Seo, Ji-Heui; Zhang, Ze; Jin, Zhenjie; Lee, Garyoung Gary; Nawfal, Rashad; Hoggood, Taylor A; Shahbazi, Sadia D; Ludwig, John; Zhang, Ziwei; Ibrahim, Elio; Nafeh, Gaelle; Berchuck, Jacob E; Sowalsky, Adam G; Karzai, Fatima; Freedman, Matthew L; Takeda, David Y; Baca, Sylvan C
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) fragmentation patterns reflect nucleosome positioning. We asked whether variation in nucleosome positions in cfDNA can reveal chromatin states and associated histone modifications. Using cell-free chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (cfChIP-seq) in plasma from patients with prostate cancer, we identified 35,120 modification-associated positions (MAPs), loci where nucleosomes bearing active (H3K4me2) and repressive (H3K9me3) histone marks occupy reproducibly offset positions. These offsets recurred across histone marks, an independent cfChIP-seq cohort, and nuclease-digested chromatin from cell lines. MAPs were enriched in transcribed genes but depleted near transcription start sites and CTCF-binding sites where nucleosome positioning is constrained. Across 2,535 cfDNA sequencing datasets, nucleosome protection at a subset of MAPs correlated with tumor fraction (TF), reflecting differences in histone modification status between cancer-derived and non-malignant chromatin. In targeted sequencing panels, a 50-MAP model using fragments from < 0.001% of the genome distinguished samples with tumor fractions >/=3% vs 0% (AUCs = 0.91-0.96 across prostate, breast, and lung cancers) and outperformed a state-of-the-art fragmentomics-based tumor fraction predictor. MAP-derived estimates correlated with reference TFs (r = 0.89) and longitudinal changes in TF (r = 0.91). MAP protection at ASCL1 binding sites identified neuroendocrine transformation of prostate cancer from cfDNA. These findings establish histone-modification-associated nucleosome positioning as a mutation-independent readout of tumor fraction and cancer state from routine cfDNA sequencing.

title: G‑quadruplexes as regulatory platforms for human transcription factors: insights from ChIP-seq data.
authors: Drapalova, Karolina; Dobrovolna, Michaela; Kledus, Filip; Mergny, Jean-Louis; Brazda, Vaclav
abstract: BACKGROUND: G-quadruplexes (G4s) are non-canonical DNA structures with important regulatory functions. While several transcription factors have been shown to interact with G4s, a comprehensive understanding of this interaction network remains elusive. RESULTS: Here, we integrated genome-wide predictions of highly stable G-quadruplex sequences with 32,817 ChIP-seq datasets from ChIP-Atlas to systematically map transcription factors and transcription-associated chromatin proteins linked to G4-rich regions in the human genome. Highly stable G4 motifs are non-randomly distributed, showing strong enrichment in gene-dense chromosomes, at promoters, regulatory regions, and repeat elements. Integration with transcription factor binding profiles revealed a broad spectrum of G4-associated proteins, including established interactors such as STAT3, TP53 and CTCF, and the transcription-associated chromatin regulator BRD4, as well as previously unrecognized candidates such as REST, NR3C1, FLI1, and HSF1. Unexpectedly, only a minority of transcription factors were consistently depleted from G4 regions. CONCLUSIONS: Our results indicate that G-quadruplex-prone sequences represent a common genomic feature associated with a number of human transcription factors and chromatin-associated regulatory proteins and support a model in which G4-rich regions act as selective regulatory scaffolds shaping transcription factor occupancy and gene regulation.

title: Truncating Kabuki Syndrome-associated KMT2D Mutation in FYR Domain Alters Chromatin Accessibility at Neurodevelopmental Loci.
authors: Ozden-Yilmaz, Gulden; Olmez, Akgun; Yilmazbilek, Irem; Tulu, Ahmet Can; Binokay, Leman; Gencpinar, Pinar; Hiz, Ayse Semra; Oktay, Yavuz; Karakulah, Gokhan; Karaca, Ezgi; Senturk, Serif; Erkek-Ozhan, Serap
abstract: Kabuki syndrome (KS) is a congenital neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by distinctive facial features, developmental delay, and multisystem involvement. KS is primarily caused by de novo mutations in KMT2D, a H3 lysine 4 (H3K4) methyltransferase within the MLL3/4 COMPASS-like complex. Although the role of KMT2D in active chromatin organization is well established, the function of its FYR domain remains largely unknown. Here, we report a KS patient carrying a heterozygous KMT2D p.R5282* nonsense mutation located at the C-terminal side of the FYR domain. The patient exhibited a relatively mild phenotype, consistent with previously reported p.R5282* mutation carriers. ATAC-seq analysis of patient-derived PBMCs revealed 451 differentially accessible regions compared to controls, with reduced accessibility mainly at promoter regions of genes involved in neurogenesis. Motif and regulatory enrichment analyses identified loss of CTCF and WRAD complex components (WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L), suggesting impaired chromatin organization. To examine the functional impact of FYR mutations, we expressed FLAG-tagged KMT2D p.R5282* and another FYR domain hotspot missense mutation (p.R5179C) in HEK293T cells and performed ATAC-seq. p.R5282*-specific chromatin changes mirrored those in the patient and were enriched for promoter regions and WRAD binding sites, whereas p.R5179C showed distinct patterns. AlphaFold3 modeling indicated that p.R5282* truncation disrupts the WIN motif required for WDR5 binding, compromising MLL3/4 complex stability. Both the patient and p.R5282*-expressing cells showed reduced chromatin accessibility at the CHD7 locus, linking KMT2D dysfunction to CHARGE syndrome pathways. These findings highlight the essential role of the KMT2D FYR domain in maintaining WRAD complex integrity and chromatin accessibility.

title: Hyperosmotic stress induces rewiring of 3D chromatin interactions.
authors: Flores, J P; Perreault, Andrea A; Drum, Zachary A; Xu, Chenxi; Alonso, Doris Cruz; Rashid, Tooba; Burgess, Jeremy D; Fox, Geoffrey C; Petros, Gelila; Wu, Yijia; Quiroga-Barber, Ivana Y; Kim, HyunAh; Sahasrabudhe, Isha; Lee, Ye Jin; Black, Ethan; Li, Yihuan; Demmerle, Justin; Strahl, Brian D; Dowen, Jill M; Wang, Gang Greg; Cai, Danfeng; Phanstiel, Douglas H
abstract: Cells continually face environmental stressors that challenge homeostasis, yet how three-dimensional (3D) chromatin structure contributes to these stress responses remains unclear under hyperosmotic conditions. To investigate this, we map 3D chromatin structure, its molecular drivers, and transcriptional outcomes during sorbitol-induced hyperosmotic stress. Within 1 hour of sorbitol treatment, pre-existing loops and domains collapse, while several hundred de novo sorbitol-induced loops emerge. These loops are punctate, longer-range, and transient. 3D chromatin structure largely returns to baseline conditions by 24 hours. Loop reorganization is consistent across cell types and hyperosmotic stimuli. Sorbitol-induced loops require cohesin but not CTCF, and anchors are enriched at active promoters harboring GC-rich transcription factor motifs. Genes at these anchors show delayed activation following loop formation, consistent with loops acting upstream of transcription. Together, hyperosmotic stress triggers rapid, reversible, CTCF-independent chromatin reorganization that correlates with transcriptional adaptation.

title: An SMN2 splicing-correcting antisense oligonucleotide promotes gene looping and transcription activation.
authors: Stigliano, Jose N; Haberfeld, Emilia; Marasco, Luciano E; Fiszbein, Ana; Proudfoot, Nick J; Kornblihtt, Alberto R
abstract: We have previously proposed a combined therapy for spinal muscular atrophy based on the upregulation of exon 7 (E7) inclusion into SMN2 mRNA by the antisense oligonucleotide nusinersen (ASO1) together with histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi). Using a CRISPR-deadCas-based strategy in a human cell line, we show here that targeting histone acetylation at the SMN2 E7 region duplicates the HDACi effect, which overcomes pleiotropic effects. Most noticeably, targeted acetylation at the E7 region causes acetylation and activation of the 30-kbp-distant promoter. Since the nusinersen target site maps near the SMN2 gene 3' end, this crosstalk between the two ends of the gene prompted us to use chromosome conformation analysis (3C) to find that ASO1 promotes gene looping. This unpredicted property of ASOs in modulating chromatin 3D configuration depends on cohesin, CTCF, cleavage/polyadenylation factors, and a canonical poly(A) signal and causes promoter activation at a long distance, which expands the therapeutic potential of splicing-correcting ASOs.

title: Bromodomain and extra-terminal motif (BET) inhibition induces coordinated repression of the stem cell-related HOX signature in glioblastoma uncovering an epigenetic vulnerability.
authors: Chiesi, Davide; Bady, Pierre; Xirouchakis, Mihalis V; Mendes Ferreira, Carla; Mohammed, Kedir S; Hegi, Monika E
abstract: BACKGROUND: Glioblastoma (GB) is the most aggressive primary brain tumor, characterized by therapy resistance, attributed to a multitude of epigenetic changes resulting in phenotypic plasticity with altered cell states. To uncover druggable epigenetic vulnerabilities, we disturbed GB-derived spheres with an inhibitor of Bromodomain and extra-terminal motif proteins (BETi) and observed coordinated repression of the aberrantly activated hemopoietic stem-like cell signature, dominated by HOXA genes. This signature has been associated with poor prognosis and resistance to therapy in GB. Here we investigate the deregulated epigenetic landscape and potential vulnerabilities in high-HOX GB. METHODS: GB-derived spheres (GS) were treated with the BETi (JQ1) or transduced with inducible constructs to genetically modulate HOXA10 expression short-hairpin (sh)RNA for knockdown, ectopic HOXA10). Functional effects were evaluated through proliferation, neurosphere formation, and senescence assays. Epigenomic profiling incorporated RNA-seq, Chromatin Immuno Precipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq), Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin sequencing (ATAC-seq), promoter capture MicroC, and DNA methylation. RESULTS: BETi-mediated rapid, coordinated downregulation of the HOX-signature suggested direct transcriptional regulation. Knockdown of HOXA10 alone yielded similar effects, decreasing expression of HOXA genes, reducing proliferation, self-renewal capacity, and triggering senescence. Conversely, ectopic HOXA10 expression failed to reactivate the HOXA cluster or reverse BETi-mediated biological effects. Integrative epigenomic analysis of high-HOX-GS revealed concerted activation of the HOXA region, with broad domains of H3K27ac/H3K4me3 associated with super-enhancer activity, open chromatin (ATAC), and focal DNA hypomethylation. Architectural changes included altered CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) interactions and increased promoter-anchored looping. CONCLUSION: These results position the HOX-signature as a potential therapeutic target and offer a mechanistic rationale for disrupting BET-dependent transcriptional regulation in high-HOX GB.

title: AxialTAD: an axial contrast architecture for TAD boundary prediction from Hi-C.
abstract: Topologically associating domains (TADs) are fundamental units of 3D chromatin organization, and accurate identification of TAD boundaries from Hi-C contact matrices remains an active challenge. Recent deep learning approaches have advanced substantially, but these rely on increasingly large architectures, raising the question of how much of this capacity boundary-centric analysis requires. Here we propose AxialTAD, a compact deep learning model centered on an Axial Contrast Module (ACM) that explicitly encodes directional contrast in contact intensity along the row and column axes of local Hi-C patches, an operator aligned with the geometric signature of TAD boundaries. Evaluated on four human cell lines (GM12878, HeLa-S3, IMR-90, K562) within cell lines and under leave-one-cell-out generalization, AxialTAD performed comparably with a recent convolutional neural network (CNN)+Transformer baseline (deepTAD) while using 76%-80% fewer trainable parameters (113K-137K versus 571K). A parameter-matched conventional CNN achieved similar F1 to AxialTAD in the human 25 kb experiments. When trained and evaluated within each of two mouse datasets, AxialTAD outperformed both this control and deepTAD. Orthogonal validation against CTCF and cohesin ChIP-seq supported the biological plausibility of the predicted boundaries. These results indicate that, within the range of architectures examined, a large architecture is not necessary to reach this level of boundary prediction.

title: NAD Metabolism Drives CTCF-Cohesin Chromatin Regulation in EBV-Transformed B-Cells
authors: Maestri D; Sklutuis R; Caruso LB; Preston-Alp S; Gatto M; Soldan SS; Park P; Melick L; Corveleyn L; Sidoli S; Kossenkov A; Goldman AR; Zhang W; Tang H; Napoletani G; Liao Y; Lieberman PM; Gewurz BE; Tempera I
abstract:
Summary

Chromatin architecture regulates gene expression, and it is maintained by architectural proteins such as CTCF and the cohesin complex. In Epstein–Barr virus infected cells, viral chromatin organization is stabilized through the interaction between PARP1 and CTCF, ensuring maintenance of latent gene expression. EBV⁺ B cells exhibit elevated PARP1 activity, which imposes a substantial metabolic burden due to NAD⁺ consumption by PARP1 itself. We demonstrate that efficient EBV infection and B-cell transformation rely on the NAD salvage pathway to sustain PARP1 activity and CTCF-cohesin chromatin folding. Pharmacologic inhibition of the rate-limiting enzyme NAMPT with FK866 phenocopies the chromatin architectural disruption induced by PARP1 and changes in NAD levels affects CTCF/cohesin chromatin architectural remodeling and loop extrusion. Moreover, NAMPT inhibition reduces tumor burden in EBV⁺ xenograft models. These findings identify a critical metabolic dependency linking NAD⁺ homeostasis to CTCF/cohesin mediated chromatin architecture and reveal a therapeutic vulnerability in EBV-associated malignancies.

title: Molecular dissection of the ChAHP complex subunits Adnp and Chd4 reveals common and divergent functions in retinal development
authors: Medisetti S; Kalinina A; Shah S; Fayaz MA; Clémot-Dupont S; Picketts DJ; Mattar P
abstract:
Epigenetic remodelling is thought to regulate the progression of competence states in neural progenitor cells. Here, we examined the functions of the ChAHP chromatin remodelling complex during retinal development. ChAHP consists of the ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeller CHD4, the zinc finger and homeodomain transcription factor ADNP, and the HP1 heterochromatin proteins (Cbx1/3/5). Notably, both CHD4 and ADNP are genetically associated with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), but ChAHP functions in neural development are not fully understood. In the retina, we found that both ADNP and CHD4 proteins were co-expressed ubiquitously in each cell type throughout development, and the two proteins formed a complex in vivo . Next, we generated retina-specific conditional knockouts (cKOs) to both Adnp and Chd4 using the Chx10-Cre driver. We observed phenotypic correspondence and divergence. Developmentally, we observed elevated cell death in both Adnp and Chd4 cKOs, but Adnp cKOs also exhibited deficits in progenitor numbers and proliferation. As a result, mature Adnp cKOs were hypoplastic with reductions in each cell type. We previously described a more complex phenotype in Chd4 cKOs, where cell fates were imbalanced and progenitor proliferation was prolonged, but these features were absent from the Adnp cKO. To understand how ChAHP regulates gene expression, we compared Adnp and Chd4 cKOs via scRNA-seq, which revealed common transcriptional signatures. However, Chd4 cKOs exhibited more severe effects on gene expression in line with its stronger effects on cell fate. We then performed cut&run-seq, which suggested that Adnp and Chd4 are recruited to the same genomic loci – many of which are also occupied by the Ctcf transcription factor. Taken together, our data suggest that ChAHP regulates retinal growth, but that CHD4 has additional ChAHP-independent functions in regulating progenitor fate decisions. These findings point to the idea that during neurogenesis, some brain regions may have greater dependence on ChAHP, and therefore greater vulnerability to genetic mutation.

Summary Statement

To investigate epigenetic processes in retinal development, we conditionally ablated the Adnp and Chd4 subunits of the ChAHP chromatin remodelling complex. Genomic, transcriptomic, and histological analyses reveal that Adnp cooperates with the nucleosome remodeller Chd4 to regulate retinal growth.

title: Local chromatin, 3D genome folding and transposon cargo shape Sleeping Beauty transposition
authors: Moene CJ; Eder M; Dauban L; Yáñez-Cuna JO; Kocher AA; Eschauzier L; Verkuilen M; Franceschini-Santos VH; van Steensel B
abstract: The cut-and-paste DNA transposon Sleeping Beauty (SB) is widely used for genome engineering, mutagenesis and gene delivery. When mobilized from a genomic donor position (“launch site”), SB preferentially reintegrates locally (< 2 Mb), but factors governing its transposition from genomic sites remain incompletely understood. Here we analysed local transposition experiments in mouse embryonic stem cells to determine the influence of chromatin context and transposon cargo on SB transposition. Transposons in launch sites with transcriptionally active, accessible chromatin showed lower transposition efficiency. Large cargo and cargo with higher transcriptional activity also result in reduced transposition efficiency. After excision, local reintegration patterns closely resembled 3D contact frequencies of the launch site. This indicates that chromosome folding is a major determinant of the transposition pattern. Surprisingly, we did not detect any effect of the destination chromatin composition on reintegration efficiency. Cargo sequence modified the reintegration patterns: promoter-containing cargo increased both very proximal (<10kb) and interchromosomal transpositions, while CTCF binding sites in the cargo increased reintegration on the launch chromosome. Together, these results define key determinants of SB transposition in chromosomes and inform the design of SB-based genome engineering strategies.

title: Genome-wide loss of chromatin accessibility coexists with selectively elevated RNA abundance in nutrient-starved U2OS cells
authors: Qi X; Al Refaai SA; Muslinov S; Panov KI
abstract:
Background

Chromatin accessibility is widely used as a proxy for regulatory potential and is often interpreted together with RNA-seq to infer gene-regulatory responses. However, the quantitative relationship between chromatin accessibility and transcript abundance may become difficult to interpret, particularly under acute cellular stress. Metabolic challenges such as nutrient deprivation are known to induce extensive chromatin remodelling and transcriptional reprogramming, raising the question of whether changes in transcript abundance are directly governed by chromatin accessibility in these contexts. Clarifying this relationship is critical for interpreting epigenomic data under stress conditions, and requires careful distinction between Tn5 accessibility, relative steady-state RNA abundance and transcriptional output.

Results

We integrated ATAC-seq and RNA-seq analyses in human U2OS osteosarcoma cells following 18 h of severe nutrient deprivation. We found that starvation was associated with a genome-wide reduction in accessibility and almost all significantly altered accessible regions showed reduced signal relative to actively growing cells. This decrease affected promoter- and enhancer-associated regions alike, including housekeeping-gene promoters and CTCF-motif sites. In contrast, RNA-seq revealed a more selective change in relative steady-state RNA abundance: only a minority of expressed genes were differentially regulated, and approximately 64% of differentially expressed genes showed increased relative RNA abundance. Changes in accessibility and transcript abundance were modestly correlated at promoters (Pearson r = 0.25) and weakly at enhancers (r = 0.10), and together explained only ∼6% of the variance in transcript abundance changes. The relationship was graded: genes with the smallest promoter losses were about four times as likely to show increased RNA abundance as genes with the largest losses, independently of baseline promoter accessibility. Within-condition analyses similarly showed only modest relationships between promoter accessibility and RNA abundance in both actively growing and starved cells. Pathway-level analysis of mRNA abundance revealed the expected repression of biosynthetic and growth-related programmes, including ribosome biogenesis, translation and cellular growth, together with a less anticipated relative activation of stress-adaptive programmes, including extracellular matrix organisation, lipid and cholesterol metabolism, small GTPase signalling and developmental processes. For genes within these activated programmes, increased steady-state mRNA abundance was observed despite reduced ATAC-seq accessibility at associated regulatory regions. Exon-intron analyses of RNA-seq data indicated that these changes predominantly reflect altered RNA production. Metabolic labelling of nascent RNA at selected loci confirmed increased transcription of genes involved in adaptive programmes despite reduced promoter and enhancer accessibility, alongside with reduced production of biosynthetic transcripts and rRNA.

Conclusions

These findings demonstrate that chromatin accessibility and steady-state RNA abundance are only modestly coupled during severe nutrient deprivation, against a baseline of similarly modest promoter accessibility-abundance coupling. This underscores the limited ability of ATAC-seq accessibility to predict transcript abundance under this stress condition and supports a model in which chromatin accessibility acts as a permissive rather than deterministic layer of gene regulation. The selective induction of adaptive programmes, confirmed here at the level of RNA production, shows that transcriptional activation can occur despite genome-wide loss of ATAC-seq accessibility. Because ATAC-seq reports Tn5 accessibility rather than physical chromatin compaction, we interpret compaction as a plausible mechanistic model compatible with the current observations, which will require direct orthogonal validation.
